opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a double-edged sword, honestly.

On one hand, having a super app like ChatGPT is an enormous asset. You have hundreds of millions of users, you have the distribution, you have the brand, and you get this incredibly rich feedback loop. Every new capability you ship, whether it's memory, or tools, or agents, you can put it in front of real people immediately and learn very fast. That's something almost no other company has. And it also gives you a kind of gravity: people already think of ChatGPT as "the place where AI lives," so anything new you add inherits that attention.

But on the other hand, a super app also creates a kind of path dependence. ChatGPT is fundamentally a chat interface. You type, it responds. That paradigm was right for a certain stage of the technology, when the main value was answering questions or writing things in one shot. But if you believe, as I do, that the next stage is more about agents doing long-horizon work, interacting with environments, working asynchronously, maybe even proactively, then the chat box is not necessarily the right form factor. And when you have a product that so many people use every day, it's very hard to radically change it. You can add features into it, but it's much harder to say, "Let's rethink the whole interaction from scratch."

It's a bit like the innovator's dilemma. The more successful your current form is, the more pressure there is to optimize it rather than replace it. Product teams naturally think, "How do we make this chat experience better?" instead of "What if the right product isn't chat at all?"

So I think what you'll see is that a company with a super app can be very strong at scaling and diffusing new capabilities, but truly new interaction modes might come from separate products, or even from other companies, that don't carry that baggage. Things like coding agents are already an example. The interface that works there looks quite different from a general chatbot. And I think there will be more of these, where the product is designed around what the model can now do, rather than around what the chat window allows.

For me, the interesting question is not just "how capable is the model," but "what is the right interface between this intelligence and humans, and between this intelligence and the world." And sometimes the biggest advantage, having the dominant product, can make it harder to see that question clearly.

r001.rationale: It explicitly describes path dependence: ChatGPT’s established chat paradigm makes it harder to rethink interaction modes from scratch.

r002.rationale: It says teams tend to improve the chat experience, but does not state that most company resources remain concentrated on that mode.

r003.rationale: It says new interaction modes may come from separate products or other companies, but does not identify startup opportunity as arising from incumbents’ focus on their super apps.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it cuts both ways, honestly.

On one hand, having something like ChatGPT is an enormous advantage. You have hundreds of millions of people already there, so when you want to try a new interaction mode, you don't have to convince anyone to download something new. You can ship a feature, and within a week you have more real-world signal than most startups would collect in their entire lifetime. That feedback loop matters a lot for agents especially, because the hard problems are not in the demo, they are in the long tail of what people actually ask for. Voice, canvas, browsing, deep research, operator-style tasks: all of these got tested at a scale that would otherwise be impossible.

On the other hand, a super app creates gravity. Once you have a chat box that works for everyone, every new idea tends to get framed as "how does this fit inside the chat box." And some interaction modes genuinely don't fit. An agent that works for you for hours in the background, or something that lives in your IDE or your operating system, is not naturally a chat turn. There's organizational pressure to not break what already works, to not confuse the existing user, to measure everything against the existing metrics. So the company becomes very good at incremental extensions of chat and less willing to make a bet that looks weird at first.

The way I think about it: chat was the right first interface because language models were, at that time, basically good at one thing, which was producing text in response to text. But as models become capable of acting over long horizons, the bottleneck shifts from the model to the environment and the interface. The question becomes what the agent can touch, how it reports back, how you supervise it. Those are design problems, not just model problems, and a super app doesn't automatically solve them. It might even make it harder to see them clearly, because the chat framing is so successful.

So my honest view is that the super app gives you distribution and data, which are huge, but the new interaction modes will probably come from people who are willing to start from the task rather than from the app. Sometimes that's a small team inside a big company that gets left alone. Sometimes it's someone outside. The interesting thing in the next couple of years is whether the big players can hold both at once: protect the super app while also letting something genuinely different grow next to it.

r001.rationale: The response says the super app creates “gravity,” framing new ideas around chat and making the company less willing to pursue unfamiliar interaction modes.

r002.rationale: It describes pressure to preserve chat and a preference for incremental extensions, but does not state that most company resources remain concentrated on the existing mode.

r003.rationale: It says new modes may come from small internal teams or outsiders, but does not identify incumbent focus on the super app as an opening for startups.

astra-6.text:
I think having a super app is both an advantage and a constraint. The advantage is that you already have users. If you develop a new capability or interaction mode, you can put it in front of people and learn very quickly whether it’s useful. You don’t have to build a distribution channel from scratch.

But a successful product also creates expectations. People open ChatGPT with a particular idea of what they’re going to do: ask a question and get an answer. So there’s a natural tendency to fit new capabilities into that existing interaction. That works for some things, but it may be limiting for an agent that needs to work for a long time, take actions, or come back to you when it needs input.

So I think the interesting question is whether the super app can become a place where different interaction modes coexist. You want to use the distribution and familiarity you already have, while still giving yourself room to discover experiences that don’t start and end with a chat message.

r001.rationale: It says a successful product creates expectations and a tendency to fit new capabilities into the existing chat interaction, communicating path dependence.

r002.rationale: It describes a tendency to fit capabilities into chat but does not say most company resources remain concentrated on that interaction mode.

r003.rationale: It does not identify this focus as an opening for startups to pursue new interaction modes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think having a super app is both an advantage and a constraint. The advantage is that you already have users, so when you develop a new capability, you can put it in front of people immediately and learn from how they use it. You don’t have to build distribution from scratch.

But it also creates a strong incentive to fit everything into the existing product. If your starting point is ChatGPT, the natural question becomes, “How do we add this to ChatGPT?” Sometimes the more useful question is, “If we built a product around this capability from the beginning, what would the interaction look like?” Those can lead to very different answers.

For example, with an agent, maybe the right interaction isn’t that you send a message and wait for a response. Maybe you delegate something, leave, and come back when it needs your input or has finished. You can support that within a chat product, but you have to be willing to rethink the assumptions behind the interface.

So I don’t think a super app prevents a company from exploring new interaction modes. The challenge is giving those explorations enough room before requiring them to fit into the successful product you already have.

r001.rationale: It says a successful super app creates a strong incentive to fit new capabilities into the existing product, shaping how the company thinks about new interactions.

r002.rationale: It describes an incentive to fit features into the existing product, but does not say that most company resources remain concentrated on the app’s existing interaction mode.

r003.rationale: It discusses the challenge of exploring new interaction modes, but does not identify that challenge as an opening for startups.
